Most AI projects fail before a single line of automation is written.
They fail in the first meeting with the vendor.

In my experience, two mistakes come first.

The company can't explain its own process.
"We want AI in sales" is a wish. A process is: who does what, in which tool, how often, and what happens when something is missing. If nobody can answer that, nobody can automate it. The vendor will guess, and you will pay for the guess.

Nobody asks which data should never reach the chat.
Client names, payments, contracts. When I built automations for a financial advisor, client data never went into the AI. The AI wrote the scripts, the scripts ran on the advisor's computer, and only summary numbers came back.

When both are clear, AI does what it's good at: the grunt work. Updating the CRM. Reminding clients about unpaid invoices. Filling in the ATS from an interview recording.

It doesn't replace the salesperson or the recruiter. It gives them hours back.

And those hours only matter if they go back to people. More interviews, faster hiring. More time with clients, fewer of them leaving.

What did your last AI project get stuck on?

Verify the report before changing your NVIDIA plans.

NVIDIA shares reportedly fell more than 7% after claims that the board was preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang. The company has not confirmed that claim, so the first practical lesson is simple: separate a market reaction from a verified governance event.

For teams buying GPUs, building AI products, or depending on CUDA, this is not a reason to pause every project. It is a reason to review concentration risk: vendor lock-in, supply commitments, hiring plans, and assumptions about NVIDIA’s pricing power.

The overlooked issue is succession risk. NVIDIA’s strategy, product cadence, and customer relationships are unusually associated with one leader. Even an unconfirmed leadership story can expose how many business plans rely on continuity that has never been tested.

This week, document which decisions depend specifically on NVIDIA: GPU availability, software compatibility, support contracts, and roadmap assumptions. Then identify one credible alternative, whether that means AMD, cloud-specific accelerators, or a smaller workload running on CPUs.

Also stop treating a stock-price move as an operating signal. Watch for a board statement, SEC filings, executive changes, and any effect on product roadmaps before making expensive technical or hiring decisions.

For thirty years, IT services grew one way: win a contract, hire people, bill for their time. More people meant more revenue.
 
AI is changing that. When software writes code and handles routine tasks, clients expect to pay less. Some are already asking their IT providers for the same work at 25 to 30% lower cost. AI also creates new demand for these firms, so even the best investors are unsure how the industry will come out of this.
 
We asked who is winning. The metric we used is revenue per employee, and whether companies can raise it while still growing revenue.
 
We looked at 37 listed IT services companies over two years. Revenue grew 6.4% and headcount 4.2%, so revenue per employee rose only 2.1%. Most of the industry still grows by hiring.
 
Plotting revenue growth against the change in revenue per employee splits the group four ways:
 
- Growing fast and earning more per person (16 companies): Accenture, Persistent Systems, Nagarro, Netcompany, Coforge, TP. They bring in half the group’s revenue with under a third of its people.
- Outliers on productivity improvement include Innodata Inc., NorthSand, Inc., Persistent Systems, Matrix IT and Nagarro
- Earning more per person but growing slowly (14): Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, HCLTech and Cognizant sit here, with about 1.7 million employees between them. TCS is close to flat on both measures.
- Shrinking to get more productive: Fujitsu, DXC Technology and Kyndryl show lower revenue but higher revenue per head, largely from cutting 10 to 15% of staff.
- Losing ground on both (5): Wipro, Capgemini, Mphasis, Cyient and Tieto
- Growing by adding people faster than revenue (2): Genpact and Hexaware Technologies.
 
When an IT company reports growth, ask two questions. Is each employee bringing in more than before? How many people will it need two years from now to earn the same amount?
 
Full analysis with charts: https://lnkd.in/gX477PPd
 
Disclaimer: Based on reported financials of 37 listed companies. Revenue per employee can also move because of job cuts or acquisitions, not only AI. For information only. Not investment advice or a recommendation to buy or sell any stock.

Everyone wants AI. But who’s going to fix the management chaos?

This isn’t a candidate’s rant. It’s about broken systems, invisible costs and opportunities businesses never notice losing. Recruitment is a symptom example.

Nine months in fintech hiring: recruiters promise next stages and vanish. Hiring takes 6+ months, then role goes on hold and reopens the new cycle soon.

One role demands strategy across five continents, 5+ years of backend engineering, business development, operations, risk and product development. C-level accountability. Specialist-level pay. 24/7 availability.

If this unicorn exists, why would they choose you? Why burn out instead of building their own business? Even nail studios show mature systems: service standards, sterilized tools and international competitions. Respect to the beauty industry.

Corporate “benefits”? Legally mandated leave and a “friendly environment” worthy of the Suicide Squad. +windowless or onlice office with a speaker on.

A broken system leaks profit like a sieve.

You can spot its culture before signing the contract. Do words match actions? Is the focus on results or micromanagement? Do KPIs reflect reality while recognizing the people behind them?

The biggest red flag isn’t a CEO having problems. It’s hearing “We have no problems” while entire teams and job titles change every year. Imagine asking on a date, “What are your flaws?” and hearing, “I have none.” There’s your answer.

In 17 years in business, I’ve worked 70-80-hour weeks, kept my phone on 24/7, jumped on a train round trip to finish a tender overnight, and written business plans at night to escape constant interruptions. I know “sink or swim” training. I can handle a crisis. But employee heroics aren't a business process.

I’ve seen exceptional leaders turn chaos into structure, hear uncomfortable truths and scale businesses through genuine win-win outcomes, same as excellent professional recruiters handling their duties on the highest standards without crossing the line.

On the other hand, broken system brings cases. Once, a strong candidate with public results heard the company’s name and said: “No, thank you.” I understood why, but couldn’t change the decisions behind that reputation.

Endless hiring, turnover, lost expertise, retraining, missed deals: these are real operating costs. But who measures the opportunities nobody even notices losing?

The 2026 AI fever reminds me of a blockchain joke from 2017:
- What’s blockchain?
- Let me explain.
- I can explain it too. But what is it?

AI is a brilliant tool in the hands of professionals who understand systems and people. AI without IQ and EQ is a grenade in a monkey’s hands. It won’t fix poor management; it may amplify it.

You can win a sprint at any cost. But will your business still be in the race a year later? Sometimes the most expensive item are not listed on a P&L as the result that never happened.

AI Agents Need Job Descriptions, Not Just Prompts

A prompt tells an AI what to do. A job description tells it what it is allowed to do, what it must never do, and who answers when something goes wrong.

The question nobody is asking?
Imagine hiring a new employee tomorrow. You give them access to your email, customer database, financial systems, cloud storage, code repository, and payment tools. Then you say: “Be helpful. Figure out the rest.”

No sensible organization would do that.
Yet that is increasingly how companies are deploying AI agents: powerful systems are connected to business tools and given broad permissions, while their purpose, limits, and accountability remain vague. The result is not a digital employee. It is an unsupervised insider with excellent language skills.

That shift from “answering questions” to “doing work” is why they need the same discipline we apply to human hiring.

Adoption is racing ahead?
The issue is whether companies are deploying them like responsible professionals or like magical black boxes with administrator access.

A prompt is not a contract
A prompt is temporary instruction. 
A job description is a durable operating agreement

The second version creates boundaries. The first creates risk.
A useful AI-agent job description should answer five questions:
1.	What is your role?
2.	What data can you access? Only the minimum data required for the task.
3.	What actions can you take? Read, draft, recommend, execute, or approve?
4.	When must you stop? High-risk actions should require human approval.
5.	Who is accountable? A named human owner, not the model.

Autonomy needs guardrails?
The most important principle is simple: an AI agent should have the least access necessary to do its job.
NIST guidance emphasizes least privilege, tightly scoped authorizations, continuous verification, and clear escalation paths when risk thresholds are reached.
This is not bureaucracy. It is basic operational hygiene.

The accountability gap
When an AI agent makes a mistake, “the AI did it” is not an acceptable answer
A strong governance model separates responsibilities:
•	Owner: Decides what the agent is for and approves its deployment.
•	Security team: Controls identity, access, logging, and monitoring.
•	Business user: Reviews outputs and handles exceptions.
•	Risk or compliance team: Defines prohibited actions and escalation rules.
•	The agent: Executes only within its defined scope.
AI can assist decisions, but it should not become the place where responsibility disappears.

In summary, An AI agent without a job description is an unmanaged risk with a polished interface. 
The Orgs that win will be those that give it the clearest purpose, the narrowest permissions, and the strongest human accountability.
AI agents do not need to be treated like humans. But they absolutely need to be managed like employees: with a role, limits, supervision, and consequences.

Two different growth models. My question remains, where are the new-logo hunters?

BUYING CAPACITY. WHO SELLS IT?

IBM Consulting ends U.S. visa and green card sponsorship for most roles.

What happens to domestic recruiting, global delivery and specialized talent availability?

Genpact: Five large net-new deals.

GDCFs are buying capabilities, expanding AI delivery and signing major deals.

A signal without its context is noise.

Qantas is cutting 850 jobs in Australia and outsourcing corporate functions to Accenture, with much of the work moving to India.
AI and technology transformation are among the reasons cited. There is an interesting contradiction here.

For years, companies outsourced work to India because labour was cheaper.
Now AI is supposed to reduce the need for labour itself.
Yet one of the world's major airlines is moving hundreds of roles to an IT services company, largely in India, while preparing for an AI-driven future.

Perhaps we are still in the transition phase.

First, work moves from expensive employees to lower-cost service providers.
Then AI and automation reduce the people needed to deliver that work.

For Indian IT services companies, this creates both an opportunity and a threat.
We may win more outsourcing contracts in the short term while gradually reducing the human effort required to service them.

And that challenges the traditional IT services model, where revenue growth has often meant hiring more people.

The next generation of IT services companies may be judged less by how many people they employ and more by how much work they deliver without adding people.
